extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric; writers and orators composing letters and speeches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing letters and prose in various rhetorical styles (plain, arid, forcible, elegant), with criteria for topic choice, structure, diction, figures, rhythm, and rhetorical effects. Useful for writers/orators deciding what suits a given addressee and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imitative conversational breaks in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent breaks in a sentence that imitate oral conversation are not appropriate in letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such imitative style better suits an actor or a speech; in writing these breaks cause obscurity. Example: lengthy conversational interruptions in Plato's dialogues are appropriate there but not in epistolary writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary revelation of character
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter should abound in glimpses of character; letters reveal the writer's soul more clearly than other forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific details and tones that let personal character show through; avoid generic impersonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep letter length within due bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of a letter must be kept within due bounds; too long letters become treatises rather than letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters that are too long and stilted read like treatises headed 'My dear So-and-So.' If addressing states or royals a slightly heightened tone may be used, but do not allow the letter to become a full treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of epistolary structure; avoid forensic periods
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter should have a certain freedom in structure; it is absurd to build up periods as if composing a courtroom speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid laboured, periodic constructions appropriate to legal oratory; 'call a spade a spade' — be direct and natural in friendly correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose topics suited to letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every subject is fitted for a letter; topics like logical subtleties or natural history are generally unsuitable for epistolary treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A letter is 'the heart’s good wishes in brief' — favour simple subjects treated simply rather than abstruse or highly technical expositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament in letters limited to friendly advice and proverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament is admissible in letters chiefly as friendly bits of kindly advice and proverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sententious maxims sparingly; excessive moralizing or sermon-like exhortations make a letter a lecture rather than friendly correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone fitted to addressee (heightening for dignitaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally letters to states or royal personages warrant a slightly heightened tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heighten style with due regard to the addressee, but stop short of transforming the letter into a treatise or a court speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'arid' style of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aridity arises from thought (trivializing momentous events), composition (excess of detached clauses), or frigid thought and tasteless expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not narrate great events with trivial words like 'in a way' or 'a nuisance'; avoid many detached clauses or abrupt aphoristic endings in contexts requiring gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate abrupt or detached clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Detached clauses and abrupt endings (aphoristic fragments) can produce aridity when used for important matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve abrupt endings for occasions that suit them; otherwise complete the members to avoid ill-timed abruptness (example: improper abrupt accusation of Aristeides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of tasteless aridity (bad thought + poor phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aridity can be compounded by bad taste in the thought together with arid wording, producing 'tasteless aridity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check both the substance (avoid frivolous or licentious ideas) and the phrasing (avoid huddled, clumsy wording) to prevent this vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of force in style
rubrics_metrics.description: Force may arise from (1) the subject-matter itself, (2) composition (concise phrasing and structure), and (3) dictional violence or harshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when the topic is inherently forcible; otherwise produce force via compact structure, short phrases, striking placement, or apt harsh diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use phrases rather than members for forcible composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In forcible style prefer phrases instead of long, multi-member clauses; brief concentrated expression heightens intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length paralyses intensity; convey much meaning in brief forms (example: Lacedaemonians' brevity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and symbolic expressions to enhance force
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity is peremptory and often more forcible; symbolic or figurative expressions can be stronger than literal expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, symbolic statements (e.g., 'your cicadas shall chirp from the ground') rather than lengthy literal descriptions to produce forceful effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic form for force; avoid looseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic (tight, rounded) sentence form is appropriate to the forcible style; loose, naive structure befits other tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring periods to a definite point at the end; avoid old-fashioned rhythms that blunt modern forcible style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid antithesis and exact symmetry when seeking force
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive antithesis and exact symmetry render style laboured, frigid, and may enfeeble invective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overdo parallel contrasts; the hearer/reader may focus on artifice rather than feeling (example: Theopompus' weakened invective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the most striking expression at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Position the most striking phrase or image at the sentence or passage end to maximize impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a striking expression is surrounded or enveloped it is blunted; the end position preserves its point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use massed short periods (two members) for sustained force
rubrics_metrics.description: A succession of short, two-member periods creates a packed, recitative forceful effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep such periods short; long-period succession brings ornament rather than force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness, reserve, and the power of silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness favors force; a sudden lapse into silence (aposiopesis) or reserve may be more powerful than explicit retort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ deliberate omission or restraint (e.g., 'I could say more but...') to heighten effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity can produce force when used judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Something distantly hinted may be more forcible than what is plainly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategic obscurity to suggest profundity or menace, but avoid unintelligibility that confuses the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cacophony and harsh diction for appropriate vigour
rubrics_metrics.description: At times harsh sounds or cacophonous diction produce vigor and suit subjects requiring harshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cacophony intentionally (example: Homeric lines using harsh order) to create a terrific effect; do not apply gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ rhetorical figures to increase force (praetermission, aposiopesis, prosopopoeia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of thought—praetermission (pretending to pass over), aposiopesis (sudden silence), prosopopoeia (personification)—enhance vehemence and drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these figures to imply magnitude, dramatize reproach, or personify abstractions (example: ancestors addressing descendants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and parallel devices (redoubling, anaphora, asyndeton)
rubrics_metrics.description: Redoubling (repeating a proper name), anaphora, asyndeton, and homoeoteleuton can powerfully emphasize and drive a passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine these devices where apt (e.g., anaphora + asyndeton + recurring termination) to produce cumulative force; beware mechanical overuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcasm, mordant wit, and ready replies as weapons of force
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash of fun, sarcasm, or mordant wit (as in Cynic speech) can contribute to force and audience response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy sarcasm or concise biting comments (e.g., Lysias' jibe about counting teeth) to create ridicule, but tailor to tone and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prolixity and ornament when seeking force
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolixity and excessive ornament suit begging/praying or florid styles, not the forcible; verbosity weakens peremptory tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor compact statement over elaborate ornamentation when aiming for power; long composed periods tend to produce ornament rather than force.
